primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: The classic Donath-Landsteiner antibody is a cold-reactive biphasic IgG autoantibody, usually directed against the P blood-group antigen. It binds RBCs and fixes complement at lower temperatures in peripheral tissues; when blood returns to 37°C, the antibody dissociates while complement activation proceeds to intravascular hemolysis.
vignette: A 6-year-old boy develops fatigue, pallor, jaundice, and dark red-brown urine one week after a self-limited viral upper respiratory infection. Hemoglobin is decreased, lactate dehydrogenase and indirect bilirubin are increased, and haptoglobin is very low. The direct antiglobulin test is positive for C3d but negative for IgG. A Donath-Landsteiner test is positive.
lead: Which mechanism best explains this patient’s hemolysis?
correct: A cold-reactive IgG antibody binds the P antigen and fixes complement at low temperature; complement-mediated lysis occurs after the blood is rewarmed
distractors: A cold-reactive IgM antibody cross-links the I antigen and causes predominantly complement-mediated extravascular hemolysis in the liver
A warm-reactive IgG antibody coats erythrocytes at 37°C and promotes Fc-mediated splenic sequestration
Oxidant stress denatures hemoglobin in erythrocytes with deficient glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
Loss of GPI-anchored CD55 and CD59 permits uncontrolled complement attack on a clonal population of erythrocytes
distractor_notes: Cold agglutinin disease is classically mediated by IgM, often anti-I, with complement fixation; it is mechanistically distinct from the biphasic Donath-Landsteiner IgG antibody of PCH.
Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia is mediated by warm-reactive IgG and predominantly splenic extravascular hemolysis; the C3-only DAT and positive Donath-Landsteiner test point elsewhere.
G6PD deficiency causes oxidant-induced hemoglobin denaturation and bite-cell/Heinz-body hemolysis rather than a complement-positive immune hemolysis.

PNH results from a PIGA-mutant hematopoietic clone lacking GPI-anchored complement regulators CD55/CD59, producing chronic/acquired complement-mediated hemolysis rather than a transient postinfectious Donath-Landsteiner syndrome.
key_expl: This child has paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria, an acute autoimmune hemolytic anemia that often follows infection in children. The classic Donath-Landsteiner antibody is a biphasic IgG autoantibody, usually anti-P. It binds erythrocytes and fixes complement in cooler peripheral blood, then dissociates as blood is rewarmed while complement activation continues, producing intravascular hemolysis. Because IgG can detach before testing, the DAT often detects complement (C3) without IgG.
objective: Distinguish paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria from cold agglutinin disease and warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia by recognizing the biphasic IgG anti-P Donath-Landsteiner mechanism.
clues: young child after recent viral illness
DAT positive for complement but negative for IgG
